title: A 1-in-a-million match. Guilty?
hook: Only 1 in a million innocent people would match. So a match means guilt. Right?

knows: counting expected cases in a population (as in the base-rates lesson)
multiplying a rate by a population size
doesNotKnow: the difference between P(match | innocent) and P(innocent | match)

misconception: If only 1 in a million innocent people would match, then someone who matches has only a one-in-a-million chance of being innocent.
objective: The learner can explain that searching N people produces about N x (1 in a million) innocent matches, so whether a match is convincing depends on how many people were searched, not just on how rare a chance match is.

claims.text: If each innocent person matches by chance with probability 1 in 1,000,000, searching 5,000,000 people gives about 5 innocent matches on average.
claims.source: Expected count = N x p = 5,000,000 x 1/1,000,000 = 5 (linearity of expectation).

claims.text: With the culprit in the database (and certain to match) plus about 5 innocent matches, a person picked out only by the match has about a 1 in 6 (roughly 17%) chance of being the culprit.
claims.source: Odds guilty : innocent among matches = 1 : 5, so P(culprit | match) is about 1/(1+5) = 0.167. Assumes the culprit is in the database, always matches, and nothing else distinguishes the matches.

claims.text: Confusing the chance that an innocent person matches with the chance that a matching person is innocent is called the prosecutor's fallacy.
claims.source: W. C. Thompson and E. L. Schumann (1987), 'Interpretation of statistical evidence in criminal trials: The prosecutor's fallacy and the defense attorney's fallacy', Law and Human Behavior 11(3): 167-187.

claims.text: In a small search the expected number of innocent matches is far below 1, so a match is much more likely to be the culprit: searching 10,000 people gives about 0.01 innocent matches.
The rings on the stage are seeded chance matches: each innocent person matches with probability 1 in 1,000,000; the seed was chosen so the full 5,000,000 search shows exactly the expected 5.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/one-in-a-million-match/model.ts: geometric gaps between matches (a Bernoulli process with p = 1e-6). Over 20,000 seeds the count in 5,000,000 people averaged 4.98 with variance 4.93 (Poisson-like, mean 5). Seed 28, picked from seeds 1-3000 to show exactly 5 spread out, puts innocent matches at about 0.56M, 1.78M, 3.12M, 4.50M and 4.82M. The culprit sits at person 417.

recall.question: A DNA profile matches 1 in 100,000 innocent people. Police search 2,000,000 profiles and find a match. Is that strong evidence on its own?
options: Yes: a 1 in 100,000 chance of innocence
No: about 20 innocent people would match too
Yes: 2 million searched makes it more reliable
recall.why: 2,000,000 x 1/100,000 = 20 expected innocent matches. The match narrows the field to about 21 people; it does not make one of them a near-certain culprit.
